anatomy.intro: White woolly areoles form the domino pattern across the rounded green ribs.

parts.function: The broad green ridge forms part of the photosynthetic stem.
parts.label: Rounded rib

parts.function: The conspicuous woolly cushion carries the tiny spines.
parts.label: White areole

parts.function: Short dark-tipped spines can be easy to overlook among the white wool.
parts.label: Tiny spine

parts.function: A small side shoot repeats the parent’s ribbed body as the plant forms a clump.
parts.label: Basal offset

flowers.text: Fragrant white funnels rise on tubes around 15–22 cm long. Each flower is short-lived, with its main display lasting about a day; the bloom can dwarf the compact body beneath it.

growth.note: Basal offsets repeat the parent’s rounded ribs and white areoles, gradually turning a single globe into a cluster.

stages.text: The compact plant shows rounded ribs and scattered white areoles.
stages.title: Single globe

stages.text: Basal shoots may gradually build a cluster around the original body.
stages.title: Widening group

stages.text: Long flower tubes can rise well beyond the small green body.
stages.title: Flowering plant

habitat.text: NParks describes the horticultural Echinopsis subdenudata from Bolivia and Paraguay. Kew places it within Echinopsis ancistrophora, whose accepted range is northwestern Argentina. The familiar nursery name and the broader taxonomic treatment remain in use side by side.

image.alt: Domino cactus with numbered rounded rib, white woolly areole, tiny dark spine and basal offset.

lookalikes.name: Astrophytum asterias
lookalikes.text: Both can look like nearly spineless dotted globes. NParks distinguishes the domino cactus’s more sharply separated ribs from the broad, flatter ribs of A. asterias.

mature.text: Individual bodies are around 7–12 cm across in the specialist description. Basal offsets increase the width of the clump while preserving its low, rounded outline.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Costa Farms.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: Martín Cárdenas published Echinopsis subdenudata in 1956. The name persists in horticulture, while Kew includes it as a synonym of Echinopsis ancistrophora.
